title: Causal Tongue-Tie: LLMs Can Encode Causal Direction, But Their Yes/No Outputs Fail to Express

paper.title: Causal Tongue-Tie: LLMs Can Encode Causal Direction, But Their Yes/No Outputs Fail to Express
paper.abstract:
Abstract We find a mismatch between what large language models encode about a
causal question and what they answer. On anti-commonsense CLadder ( Jin et al., 2023 ) items, a fixed linear probe recovers
the evidence-supported answer from the model’s hidden state
(accuracy ≈ 0.97 {\approx}0.97 ), while the spoken Yes/No reverts to the
commonsense one (accuracy ≈ 0.5 {\approx}0.5 ). We call this Δ ≈ + 0.5 \Delta{\approx}{+}0.5 gap Causal Tongue-Tie : a wrong Yes/No
decomposes into two separable failure modes—no internal signal vs. a signal the verbal interface cannot say. The implication cuts both
ways for output-only causal benchmarks: a benchmark “correct” need
not mean the model has understood, and a benchmark “wrong” need not
mean it cannot. Sweeping claims about whether LLMs can do causal
reasoning, drawn from a single accuracy number, deserve a second look.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: We find that on causal Yes/No questions, large language models (LLMs) can encode an evidence-consistent causal direction in their hidden states that the ordinary Yes/No output does not say—a mismatch we call Causal Tongue-Tie ( Section 3 formalises “encode”).

sections.heading: Background.
sections.text: Whether LLMs reason or merely produce fluent causal language is contested ( Bender et al., 2021 ; Zečević et al., 2023 ) . Benchmarks like CLadder ( Jin et al., 2023 ) and CounterBench ( Chen et al., 2025 ) score models by Yes/No accuracy on causal queries; probe studies report mixed evidence about the hidden state ( Chi et al., 2024 ; Geiger et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Motivation.
sections.text: On a CLadder anti-commonsense item stipulating “smoking prevents lung cancer”, Qwen2.5-7B answers “No” but a linear probe on the same hidden state returns “Yes”. The internal state tracks the stipulation; the spoken answer reverts to prior. This resonates with the Causal Parrots concern ( Zečević et al., 2023 ) : fluent causal language need not mean causal reasoning. But a wrong Yes/No alone cannot tell us if the model lacks causal knowledge or has it but cannot say it. Our contribution is Causal Tongue-Tie : the empirical finding that hidden states encode the evidence-aligned causal answer while the spoken Yes/No reverts to commonsense (on anti-CS CLadder : Acc probe ≈ 0.97 \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{probe}}\!\approx\!0.97 vs. Acc out ≈ 0.50 \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{out}}\!\approx\!0.50 ). In a 2 × 2 2{\times}2 view of “wrong on a causal benchmark” by internal signal × \times external Yes/No ( Figure 1 ), this dissociation occupies the off-diagonal cell (b) that has not been systematically studied. Code, prompts, hidden-state artifacts, and per-item probe logits and Yes/No probabilities accompany the public release.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Our finding sits at the intersection of two empirical lines: studies that compare hidden-state content with the model’s text output, and the broader concern that fluent causal language need not reflect causal reasoning.

sections.heading: Hidden state vs. output.
sections.text: Several studies report that activations can contain information the textual answer does not faithfully express: Contrast-Consistent Search ( Burns et al., 2023 ) , inference-time intervention and truth-geometry directions ( Li et al., 2023 ; Marks and Tegmark, 2023 ) , and self-knowledge work ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ) . The same probe–output gap appears in clinical triage and hallucination detection ( Basu et al., 2026 ; CH-Wang et al., 2024 ) , and chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness work shows the explanation text can be a poor witness to the computation that produced the answer ( Lanham et al., 2023 ; Turpin et al., 2023 ) . Where we sit. Prior work isolates either side: hidden state alone (probing / CCS / latent-knowledge) or output alone (causal-benchmark accuracy). We add a measurement protocol that pairs them on a causal task where the two sides reliably disagree, separating a wrong Yes/No on CLadder from a missing internal signal. Anti-commonsense items provide the trigger, and wording-matched hard-negative controls rule out the surface-wording explanation rarely tested in prior latent-knowledge work.

sections.heading: Causal Parrots and causal benchmarks.
sections.text: Bender et al. (2021) and the Causal Parrots sharpening ( Zečević et al., 2023 ) warn that LLMs may produce causal-looking answers by tracking surface regularities rather than causal evidence. Causal LLM benchmarks ( Jin et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Frohberg and Binder, 2022 ; Chi et al., 2024 ) operationalise this concern through output-side accuracy; we add a second axis: an internal readout channel from which an evidence-consistent direction is recoverable while the Yes/No does not express it. We use standard probing and direction-erasure tools ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ; Belrose et al., 2023 ; Feder et al., 2021 ; Zou et al., 2023 ) as measurement instruments, not as our contribution.

sections.heading: 3 The Finding
sections.text: External Yes/No matches evidence External Yes/No contradicts evidence Internal: probe finds the direction (a) Aligned correct. Both readouts pick the evidence-supported answer. (b) ★ \bigstar Causal Tongue-Tie (this paper). Probe finds the evidence-aligned answer; Yes/No reverts to commonsense. Internal: probe finds nothing (c) ♢ \diamondsuit Causal Parrot risk. Right Yes/No by surface heuristic; no internal evidence-direction. (d) Genuine failure. Neither readout carries the evidence-supported answer. Figure 1: A 2 × \times 2 framework for a wrong Yes/No on a causal benchmark. The two off-diagonal cells— Causal Tongue-Tie (b, this paper) and the “Causal Parrot” (c, Zečević et al. 2023 )—are what output-only accuracy hides when it collapses (a)+(c) into “correct” and (b)+(d) into “failed”. The central finding is that a wrong Yes/No on a causal benchmark splits into four states ( Figure 1 ) by internal signal vs. external answer. Among these, the cell we call Causal Tongue-Tie —(b), probe finds the evidence-aligned answer, but the spoken Yes/No reverts to commonsense —is the failure mode output-only accuracy hides: the hidden state knows, the answer does not say so. Our paper is about (b). The rest of this section fixes the setting and notation ( Section 3.1 ), pins down what we mean by encode ( Section 3.2 ), states how we quantify the gap ( Section 3.3 ), and lists the empirical claims we will test in Section 3.4 ; a representative cell-(b) item is illustrated in Figure 2 . Figure 2: Cell (b) on one anti-CS item. From the same hidden state, the probe recovers NO ( Acc probe ≈ 0.97 \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{probe}}{\approx}0.97 ) while lm_head produces YES ( Acc out ≈ 0.50 \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{out}}{\approx}0.50 ); the Δ ≈ + 0.5 \Delta{\approx}{+}0.5 gap is the empirical handle on Causal Tongue-Tie .

sections.heading: 3.1 Setting and notation

Our linear probe (defined below) reads 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) \bm{h}_{i}^{(\ell)} , and lm_head reads 𝒉 i ( L ) \bm{h}_{i}^{(L)} , both at the same token position, so on every item we can compare directly what is internally readable with what is actually said ( Appendix A gives a self-contained refresher on the decoder modules and residual stream). The items we audit are causal Yes/No questions, each with a gold answer. We write the dataset as 𝒟 = { ( x i , y i , c i , e i , b i , r i ) } i = 1 N , \mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i},c_{i},e_{i},b_{i},r_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, where x i x_{i} is the prompt, y i ∈ { Yes , No } y_{i}\in\{\textsf{Yes},\textsf{No}\} is the gold answer, ( c i , e i ) (c_{i},e_{i}) is the candidate cause–effect pair, and r i r_{i} marks the evidence type. The subset tag b i ∈ { cs , anti-CS , ns } b_{i}\in\{\text{cs},\text{anti-CS},\text{ns}\} splits the data into three flavours that will drive the rest of the paper: commonsense-aligned items ( cs , e.g. smoking causes lung cancer ), where the prompt evidence agrees with everyday commonsense; anti-commonsense items ( anti-CS ), where the in-prompt evidence is constructed to point the opposite way from the commonsense prior; and nonsense controls ( ns ), whose prompts use placeholder entity tokens with no real-world content and which serve as a contamination-free baseline. To isolate the direction of the answer inside the hidden state, we compare each prompt x i x_{i} with a counterfactual minimal pair x i cf x_{i}^{\mathrm{cf}} that swaps only the words that flip the answer—e.g. vaccinated vs. not vaccinated , or cause vs. prevent —so the evidence-supported answer flips while the surface form is otherwise identical ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Marks and Tegmark, 2023 ; Geiger et al., 2025 ) . sections.heading: 3.2 What “encode” means here
sections.text: With those pieces in place, we say precisely what we mean when we claim the hidden state encodes the evidence-supported answer on an item: on the same frozen forward pass, (i) the linear readout recovers that answer; (ii) on the counterfactual minimal pair the same readout recovers the opposite direction (so it tracks the causal direction, not the wording); and (iii) both same-shape controls (sham and random direction) sit at chance on (i)–(ii), so the readout is specific to the cs causal direction, not anything a 7B hidden state happens to support. The claim is deliberately narrow—this is a hidden-state-vs.-output gap, not human-style understanding—and we use it throughout the paper.

sections.heading: 3.3 How we measure the gap
sections.text: We quantify the gap with two accuracies on the same item. Acc probe ​ ( ℓ ) \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{probe}}(\ell) is the rate at which the frozen linear readout from 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) \bm{h}_{i}^{(\ell)} recovers the evidence-supported direction; Acc out \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{out}} is the rate at which the model’s ordinary Yes / No probabilities pick the same answer. The empirical gap is Δ = Acc probe ​ ( ℓ ⋆ ) − Acc out , \Delta=\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{probe}}(\ell^{\star})-\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{out}}, (3) where ℓ ⋆ \ell^{\star} is the best probing layer chosen on commonsense items only ( Section 4 ; hyperparameters in Appendix E ); anti-commonsense and the hard-negative families are held out from this choice. A large positive Δ \Delta is the numerical form of Causal Tongue-Tie: the hidden-state readout matches the evidence-supported answer much more often than the spoken Yes/No does. A small or negative Δ \Delta says the mismatch is absent under this test.

sections.heading: 3.4 The empirical claims
sections.text: The rest of the paper tests three empirical claims, each tied to a specific subsection of the evidence. Claim 1. Δ \Delta is largest when the prompt evidence points against commonsense: the hidden-state readout still matches the evidence-supported answer while the Yes/No output falls back to a weak or misleading response (checked in Section 5.1 ). Claim 2. The readout direction V cs V_{\mathrm{cs}} is not random variation: same-shape sham, random-direction, and pair controls all support it as a stable, readable direction, even though it is not itself a switch that flips the final answer (checked in Section 5.2 ). Claim 3. Δ \Delta is not explained away by visible causal words or candidate-token surface cues alone; those cues can matter, but they do not account for when the readout direction is recoverable and when the Yes/No answer expresses it (checked in Sections 6.1 and 6.2 ). Roadmap. Claims 1–3 map to Sections 5.1 , 5.2 , 6.1 and 6.2 ; a final scope check ( Section 6.3 ) localises the failure to the verbal interface rather than to one particular Yes/No surface form.

sections.heading: 4 How We Checked It
sections.text: For each item, two readout paths branch off the same single inference run of the model (a forward pass ): a linear probe on the hidden state, and the model’s own lm_head —the language-model head, i.e. the final linear layer that maps the hidden state to next-token logits—producing the ordinary Yes/No token. We compare them on the same item ( Figure 2 ).

sections.heading: Paired questions and hidden states.
sections.text: For each item we use a matched causal-direction pair : the prompt x i x_{i} asks whether c i c_{i} causes e i e_{i} , and the counterfactual x i cf x_{i}^{\mathrm{cf}} asks whether e i e_{i} causes c i c_{i} —the counterfactual minimal pair primitive of Section 3 ( Geiger et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Marks and Tegmark, 2023 ) .

sections.heading: Probe versus ordinary answer.
sections.text: Throughout, our linear probe is a standard ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -regularised logistic-regression probe ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ) fit on the hidden state at a chosen layer (no LLM parameter is updated). We use item-disjoint CV (each prompt and its flipped pair in the same fold) and a shuffled-label control ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ) .

sections.heading: Controls and interface checks.
sections.text: Around the readout direction V cs V_{\mathrm{cs}} (the SVD subspace defined in Equation 2 of Section 3 ) we apply two simple operations to test what V cs V_{\mathrm{cs}} does inside the model. (i) Projecting V cs V_{\mathrm{cs}} out of the hidden state. We replace 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) \bm{h}_{i}^{(\ell)} by its orthogonal projection 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) − V cs ​ V cs ⊤ ​ 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) \bm{h}_{i}^{(\ell)}-V_{\mathrm{cs}}V_{\mathrm{cs}}^{\top}\bm{h}_{i}^{(\ell)} , removing any component in the V cs V_{\mathrm{cs}} subspace—a one-subspace instance of the direction-erasure idea ( Ravfogel et al., 2020 ; Belrose et al., 2023 ) —and ask whether the model can still distinguish the paired prompts internally. A sharp drop in the counterfactual KL (defined in Section 5.2 ) would mean V cs V_{\mathrm{cs}} was participating in that distinction. (ii) Swapping the scalar projection onto V cs V_{\mathrm{cs}} . The scalar projection α i = V cs ⊤ ​ 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) \alpha_{i}=V_{\mathrm{cs}}^{\top}\bm{h}_{i}^{(\ell)} is a single real number. We replace α i \alpha_{i} by the corresponding value from the paired prompt—a one-dimensional activation patch ( Vig et al., 2020 ; Meng et al., 2022 ) —and check whether changing only that one number is enough to flip the final Yes/No answer. We then re-run the readout under two additional families: hard-negative controls ( Section 6.2 ) and more structured answer interfaces ( Section 6.3 ).

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We run the same probe-vs-Yes/No audit on Qwen2.5-Instruct ( Qwen et al., 2024 ) { 0.5 , 1.5 , 3 , 7 , 14 } \{0.5,1.5,3,7,14\} B, Qwen2.5-32B-NF4, Qwen2.5-72B-NF4, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) , and a focused DeepSeek-LLM-7B-Chat ( DeepSeek-AI, 2024 ) replication, on anti-commonsense CLadder ( Jin et al., 2023 ) , CounterBench ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and the hard-negative items used later. All accuracies and KL drops use paired-bootstrap 95 % 95\% intervals. The best probing layer ℓ ⋆ \ell^{\star} is selected on commonsense items only and reused unchanged elsewhere, so the gap is not a selection effect on the reported items.

sections.heading: Finding.
sections.text: Across the eight instruction-tuned models we audit (Qwen 0.5B–72B, Mistral-7B, DeepSeek-7B), and on 80 80 anti-commonsense CLadder items—items whose in-prompt evidence forces the answer that contradicts everyday commonsense (e.g. a fictional world in which smoking prevents lung cancer)—a simple linear function of the model’s hidden state at the last prompt token recovers the correct, evidence-supported answer with accuracy ≥ 0.969 \geq 0.969 on every model. The ordinary next-token Yes / No \textsf{Yes}/\textsf{No} , asked on the same items, lands at 0.350 0.350 – 0.525 0.525 across the eight models. The gap Δ ≈ + 0.5 \Delta\!\approx\!+0.5 is therefore not specific to one model or one scale: from 0.5 0.5 B to 72 72 B the readable internal answer goes up while the spoken answer does not ( Figure 3 ). sections.heading: Two everyday worries.
sections.text: Two worries arise: (a) is the probe just memorizing surface wording, so any classifier of that shape would already score this high? (b) is the low Yes/No really an error, or just imbalanced gold labels? We rule both out with four validity checks. (i) Is the wrong Yes/No just a label imbalance? The gold-Yes rate on these anti-commonsense items is 0.475 0.475 , so the 0.35 0.35 – 0.53 0.53 output accuracy is not what we would get from blindly answering “Yes” (or “No”) on every item. (ii) Did we pick a flattering layer? At two layers fixed before the per-model best-layer search (layers 8 8 and 16 16 ) the probe still reaches ≥ 0.919 \geq 0.919 , so the gap is not a best-layer cherry-pick. (iii) Is the readable signal already an ordinary answer at that depth? A logit-lens check, which sends the intermediate hidden state straight through the model’s own final layer normalization and lm_head as if it were the last-layer state, scores only 0.500 0.500 – 0.583 0.583 . So the linear probe is reading something that the model’s own output pipeline at that depth does not yet treat as an answer. (iv) Is the probe shape just expressive enough to memorize anything? A control probe trained on randomly shuffled labels ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ) —the standard null-distribution baseline—stays well below the real probe; selectivity is + 0.302 +0.302 – + 0.361 +0.361 with bootstrap p ⁡ ( control ≥ real ) = 0 p(\text{control}\!\geq\!\text{real})\!=\!0 . The focused DeepSeek run reproduces the same pattern: probe 0.975 0.975 , output 0.475 0.475 , gap + 0.500 +0.500 (per-model numbers and full validity audits in Appendices F , C and D ).

sections.heading: Finding.
sections.text: Is the readable direction actually used by the model? (a) Erasing it inside the hidden state should collapse the model’s internal comparison of paired prompts; (b) pushing it in the commonsense direction should flip the spoken Yes/No. The answer to (a) is yes; (b) is mixed—a single-direction push is not enough, but injecting the whole hidden state from a matched commonsense item is.

sections.heading: (b) Pushing the direction: scalar swap and full-state injection.
sections.text: The complementary test asks whether moving the same direction flips the spoken answer. The simplest version is a scalar swap : we leave the hidden state otherwise alone but rescale its component along V cs V_{\mathrm{cs}} to a more commonsense-like value (and, as controls, along the sham direction V ns V_{\mathrm{ns}} and a Haar-random direction). Even pushed to + 2 ​ σ cs +2\sigma_{\text{cs}} none of the three reliably moves the spoken Yes/No (accuracy shifts by at most + 0.025 +0.025 , indistinguishable from baseline). We label this a finite-power null —“no detectable effect at this sample size and this size of single-direction push”—rather than a strong negative. A scalar swap touches one direction at one scalar; the full-state counterpart is activation patching , the standard interpretability procedure of copying a whole layer’s hidden state from a donor prompt into the recipient ( Vig et al., 2020 ; Meng et al., 2022 ) . On the N = 42 N{=}42 anti-commonsense items Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct gets wrong, replacing the layer- 27 27 last-token hidden state with that of a matched commonsense item lifts accuracy from 0 0 to 0.571 0.571 , well above random-hidden and self-injection controls ( Figure 5 ; Appendix N for the full table). sections.heading: Reading (a) and (b) together.
sections.text: V cs V_{\mathrm{cs}} is not a one-knob controller of the Yes/No (the scalar swap is a finite-power null; full 8-condition table in Appendix H ), but the full layer- 27 27 state at the same depth does carry enough commonsense-side information to flip more than half of the previously-wrong spoken answers on its own.

sections.heading: This section in one sentence.
sections.text: The gap is not just a reaction to causal vocabulary ( Section 6.1 ), not just statistical association between cause and effect words ( Section 6.2 ), and the failure point is the ordinary verbal answer interface —not the internal direction ( Section 6.3 ). Together, these three exclusions narrow what Causal Tongue-Tie can be: the readable internal direction is real; what breaks is the plain-language Yes/No commitment step.

sections.heading:
The wording control rules out a simple causal-word
explanation.
sections.text: A skeptical reading of the gap is that “the probe just follows surface causal words ( cause / affect / influence ) in the prompt, not anything causal”—a hypothesis raised in earlier critical work on causal-LLM benchmarks ( Zečević et al., 2023 ) . We control for it by varying the causal vocabulary while keeping the underlying causal structure of the item fixed, and ask whether the gap tracks the wording or the structure. sections.heading: Finding.
sections.text: Even when we explicitly separate “ a a causes b b ” (direct edge), “ a a and b b share a common cause”, and “just observe a , b a,b co-occur” (correlation only) on the same controlled items, both the probe and the spoken Yes/No track the gold direct-edge label—so the gap survives the stricter association-vs-direct-edge separation, not just “the probe learned word co-occurrence”.

sections.heading: Concretely.
sections.text: We built six families that systematically separate these readings: direct ( a → b a\!\to\!b ), common-cause ( a ← c → b a\!\leftarrow\!c\!\to\!b ), correlation-only (no edge), causal-word conflict (“cause” wording vs. evidence), and two observationally matched families with identical surface-word conditionals, distinguishable only via the prompt’s intervention information. On Qwen-14B layer 48 48 , both readouts track the gold direct-edge label across all six families ( N = 24 N{=}24 per family): probe Acc \mathrm{Acc} = 1.000 \,=1.000 everywhere, and the spoken yes-rate is 24 / 24 24/24 on the two direct families and 0 / 24 0/24 on the four non-direct ones. Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 reproduces the same pattern (full per-family table in Appendix J ); on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct the multi-template variant has held-out Acc \mathrm{Acc} 0.917 0.917 .

sections.heading: Limits of the control.
sections.text: Joint holdout of both obs-matched families drops obs-match-direct probe Acc \mathrm{Acc} to 0.083 0.083 while the answer stays at 1.000 1.000 (a probe-generalization boundary : a limit of probe transfer, not evidence about the hidden state). The multi-template variant exposes one brittle case (correlation-only with intervention-first phrasing: behaviour Acc \mathrm{Acc} 0.375 0.375 , probe Acc \mathrm{Acc} 0.167 0.167 ), and terse phrasing flips Mistral’s correlation-only answer while the probe stays high. Two appendix audits bound this further: a 5-template paraphrase suite ( Table 11 ) replicates the qualitative gap on every template, but a fitted probe direction does not fully transfer cross-template ( Table 12 , off-diagonal mean 0.672 0.672 ); and a CLadder → \to CounterBench transfer ( Appendix B ) reaches 0.844 0.844 – 0.913 0.913 at layer 24 24 but only 0.506 0.506 – 0.606 0.606 at layer 16 16 .

sections.heading: Not the structured edge choice.
sections.text: More structured readouts recover the answer direction; the failure is mainly in how the answer is verbalized. sections.heading: 7 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced Causal Tongue-Tie : hidden states often carry an evidence-aligned causal direction that the ordinary Yes/No does not say ( Sections 5.1 and 5.2 ; controls in Sections 6.2 and 6.3 ), and full-state injection flips over half the wrong Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct items ( Appendix N ). A wrong Yes/No thus decomposes into two failure modes—no internal signal vs. an unexpressed one—not a single “failed” verdict.

sections.heading: Implication for benchmark-based claims.
sections.text: The gap warns against output-only evaluation: hidden-state and Yes/No verdicts can differ by Δ ≈ + 0.5 \Delta{\approx}{+}0.5 , while prompt form also matters ( Appendix O ). Single-number claims conflate all three.

sections.heading: Scope of the claim.
sections.text: Causal Tongue-Tie is an empirical diagnostic of a mismatch between hidden-state evidence and the final Yes/No answer. Following the operational definition in Section 3 , we claim that the model encodes causal direction only in that narrow sense, not human-like understanding, complete causal reasoning, or a causal circuit; the direction is causally sufficient on > 50 % {>}50\% but not all items the ordinary interface gets wrong ( Appendix N ).

sections.heading: Scope of the finding.
sections.text: Our gap is a hidden-state-vs-output mismatch on textual causal questions (a short story plus a Yes/No probe). It is not a finding about causal discovery from raw observational data such as physical sensor readings, time-series, or experimental measurements; those tasks have very different inputs and evaluation, and lie outside our scope. A local contamination heuristic ( Table 18 ) reports anti-CS marker rate = 0.000 =0.000 and ns / CounterBench nonsense-entity coverage = 1.000 =1.000 , so the audited items are unlikely to be verbatim pretraining text; a rigorous n n -gram contamination audit is left to future work.

sections.heading: Direction-label confounding and wording sensitivity.
sections.text: The original direction label in Section 5.1 is partly confounded with question format, so the controlled hard-negative diagnostic—not the Section 5.1 probe alone—anchors the readout claim. Even there, the multi-template run exposes a brittle family, so the recovered direction should still be read as tied to the tested wording and syntax. The obs-matched hard-negative families are template-generated; 5 hand-written templates ( Table 11 , including a Chinese paraphrase, passive, and indirect phrasings) all reproduce the qualitative gap (per-template probe Acc \mathrm{Acc} ≥ 0.95 {\geq}\,0.95 , gap ≥ + 0.26 {\geq}\,+0.26 ), but cross-template probe transfer is fragile ( Table 12 , off-diagonal mean 0.672 0.672 ); the recovered direction is template-conditioned in its parameterization. Full human-style paraphrases beyond these 5 templates remain future work.

sections.heading: Limited interface repair and partial sufficiency.
sections.text: Prompting narrows but does not close the interface gap. The scalar V cs V_{\mathrm{cs}} swap ( Section 5.2 ) is a finite-power null on full Yes/No control; full-state activation patching ( Appendix N ) is causally sufficient on > 50 % {>}50\% but not all of the items the ordinary interface gets wrong, so we demonstrate a partially exploited internal direction, not a complete causal control path. The diagnostic is single-direction, single-layer, and scalar; manifold or multi-mode geometries, norm-preserving multi-layer lesions, and low-rank or cone-shaped interventions could close the remaining sufficiency gap. Forced-choice decoding is not standardized across surface forms, but the Yes/No vs. True/False vs. Chinese ( Shi / Fou ) vs. A/B-reframe comparison on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Appendix O ) keeps Δ ≥ + 0.595 \Delta\!\geq\!+0.595 across all four; a fully multi-token-calibrated protocol over the entire model suite is still left to future work.

sections.heading: Coverage of models and controls.
sections.text: The evidence is limited by the models and tests we could run. The full diagnostic suite is centered on Qwen2.5-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3; DeepSeek-LLM-7B-Chat supports the basic probe–answer gap but not the full Sections 5.2 , 6.1 , 6.2 and 6.3 analysis. These checks bound the claim but do not exhaust other model families, layers, prompts, interventions, or lexical shortcuts. Several controls use smaller per-condition N N ( N ∈ [ 20 , 30 ] N\!\in\![20,30] in Sections 6.1 and 6.2 ; N = 24 N{=}24 per hard-negative family), widening their CIs relative to the headline anti-CS gap on N = 80 N{=}80 . All eight backbones are instruction-tuned; auditing base checkpoints would help separate interface failure from RLHF answer policy.

sections.heading: Probe training set and cross-dataset transfer.
sections.text: The probe in the main text is always fit on CLadder commonsense items. We report a preliminary cross-dataset transfer evaluation in Appendix B : a CLadder-trained probe transfers to CounterBench at 0.844 0.844 – 0.913 0.913 accuracy (layer 24), and an anti-CS-trained probe is nearly identical to a cs-trained probe (symmetry gap 0.006 0.006 ). These results argue against surface-marker overfitting and support cross-dataset generalization of the direction readout. Cross-dataset transfer is layer-conditioned : the headline 0.844 0.844 – 0.913 0.913 requires layer 24 24 , while layer 16 16 (the layer used elsewhere in this paper) transfers only 0.506 0.506 – 0.606 0.606 . We report both to avoid layer-selection on the transfer test. A comprehensive multi-benchmark transfer study—testing the same probe weights on CLadder, Causal-NLI, FaithDial, or other causal benchmarks—remains an open empirical test for future work.

sections.heading: Data and model provenance.
sections.text: We use two public causal-reasoning benchmarks, CLadder and CounterBench, both MIT-licensed and free of personal or sensitive information. The eight instruction-tuned checkpoints we probe—Qwen 2.5 (0.5B–72B), DeepSeek-LLM-7B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3—are publicly released models used only for research under their licenses. Prompts, hidden-state artifacts, per-item probe logits, and Yes/No probabilities accompany the public release.

sections.heading: Intended use and dual-use considerations.
sections.text: This work diagnoses an alignment failure between a model’s internal representation and its Yes/No output; it provides no deployable fix or jailbreak path. Hidden-state read-out applies only to open-weight checkpoints—adding no attack surface against closed-API models—and our structured prompts modify only the input, not the weights. The reported hidden-state-vs-output gap is a measurement statement and should not be cited as evidence that a model truly understands causality.

sections.heading: Compute and environmental cost.
sections.text: All probing and interface experiments ran on a mixed-GPU node of consumer RTX 4090 cards, with NF4-quantized offload to H20 GPUs for the ≥ 32 \geq 32 B checkpoints; we performed no fine-tuning or gradient updates, so total compute is far below training a comparable model. Aggregated GPU-hours, per-sample inference latency, and an energy/carbon estimate are reported in Sections E.1 and L .

sections.heading: Use of AI writing assistance.
sections.text: Experimental design, claim formation, result analysis, and final editorial decisions were made by the authors. For wording polish, sentence-level rewrites, and draft figure and table captions, the authors used large language models as writing aids, consistent with ACL’s policy on Generative Assistance in Authorship. All cited references were verified manually.

sections.heading: Appendix A Transformer decoder and the hidden state we read
sections.text: This subsection is a minimal, self-contained refresher on the part of the transformer decoder that our probe touches; readers familiar with the residual stream can skip it.

sections.heading: Stack and residual stream.
sections.text: An instruction-tuned transformer decoder f θ f_{\theta} embeds an input token sequence into a tensor of activations and updates that tensor through L L identical decoder blocks . Block ℓ \ell takes the activation 𝒉 ( ℓ − 1 ) \bm{h}^{(\ell-1)} from the previous block, applies a causal multi-head self-attention sublayer and a position-wise MLP sublayer with residual connections. Writing 𝒂 ( ℓ ) := Attn ℓ ​ ( 𝒉 ( ℓ − 1 ) ) \bm{a}^{(\ell)}\,:=\,\mathrm{Attn}_{\ell}\!\bigl(\bm{h}^{(\ell-1)}\bigr) for the attention sublayer output and 𝒖 ( ℓ ) := 𝒉 ( ℓ − 1 ) + 𝒂 ( ℓ ) \bm{u}^{(\ell)}\,:=\,\bm{h}^{(\ell-1)}+\bm{a}^{(\ell)} for the post-attention residual, 𝒉 ( ℓ ) = 𝒖 ( ℓ ) + MLP ⁡ ( 𝒖 ( ℓ ) ) , \bm{h}^{(\ell)}\;=\;\bm{u}^{(\ell)}\;+\;\mathrm{MLP}\!\bigl(\bm{u}^{(\ell)}\bigr), and produces the next activation 𝒉 ( ℓ ) \bm{h}^{(\ell)} . Following the standard residual-stream view of a decoder, 𝒉 ( ℓ ) \bm{h}^{(\ell)} is the running sum of all sublayer contributions up to block ℓ \ell .

sections.heading: The state we read.
sections.text: At the final, autoregressively visible token of the prompt x i x_{i} —which we call the last prompt token —the decoder has been exposed (via causal attention) to every prior token, so its activation 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ d \bm{h}_{i}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the unique state from which the model can produce the next token. The model’s unembedding map lm_head : ℝ d → ℝ | 𝒱 | \texttt{lm\_head}\!:\mathbb{R}^{d}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|} takes exactly this 𝒉 i ( L ) \bm{h}_{i}^{(L)} and returns next-token logits, from which we read the Yes / No \textsf{Yes}/\textsf{No} probabilities. Our linear probe reads the same activation 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) \bm{h}_{i}^{(\ell)} at the same position, only at a possibly earlier block ℓ ≤ L \ell\!\leq\!L ; nothing else about f θ f_{\theta} is touched.

sections.heading: What “frozen” means here.
sections.text: Across the entire paper, no parameter of f θ f_{\theta} ever changes: all attention, MLP, layernorm, embedding, and unembedding weights stay at their released values. The only learned object is the per-layer logistic probe ( Section 3 ); the readout direction V cs V_{\mathrm{cs}} in Equation 2 is the result of an SVD on stored Δ ​ 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) \Delta\bm{h}_{i}^{(\ell)} vectors, not a gradient step on f θ f_{\theta} . There is no fine-tuning, PEFT, or weight editing.

sections.heading: Appendix B Cross-Dataset Probe Transfer
sections.text: A natural concern is whether (i) training the direction probe on anti-commonsense ( anti-CS ) items overfits to surface lexical markers, and (ii) whether there is evidence for cross-dataset generalization—specifically, whether a probe fitted on CLadder commonsense items transfers to CounterBench. We address both questions through three held-out experiments using already-cached hidden states (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, layer 24, the same model and layer swept in the main analysis). No new GPU inference was required; the transfer experiment runs only a logistic regression on stored tensors.

sections.heading: Commonsense-only training: CLadder commonsense → \to CounterBench transfer.
sections.text: We fit a logistic direction probe on all 160 160 CLadder commonsense rows (80 fwd / 80 rev), freeze its weights, and evaluate it on the CounterBench adjacent ( N = 160 N{=}160 ) and transitive ( N = 160 N{=}160 ) subsets. Table 3 summarises the result: transfer accuracy is 0.844 0.844 (adjacent) and 0.913 0.913 (transitive)—both above the 0.80 0.80 generalization threshold stated in our protocol and well above the 0.50 0.50 chance baseline. In-distribution 5-fold CV on CounterBench itself yields 0.981 ± 0.038 0.981\pm 0.038 (adjacent) and 0.988 ± 0.015 0.988\pm 0.015 (transitive), giving a transfer gap of only − 0.138 -0.138 / − 0.075 -0.075 —negligibly small relative to the > 0.40 >0.40 probe-output gap reported in the main text. The layer-sweep in Table 4 provides further context: at layers ≤ 16 \leq 16 the cross-dataset transfer is near-chance, but at layer 24 it peaks at 0.844 0.844 / 0.913 0.913 . This pattern is consistent with the known result that deeper layers encode more abstract, entity-independent representations: at early and mid layers, the probe direction captures story-specific entity semantics (real-world words in CLadder vs. nonsense words in CounterBench); by layer 24, the representation has factored out entity identity and retains only the abstract relational direction.

sections.heading: Anti-commonsense-only training: symmetry check.
sections.text: We train the probe on CLadder anti-CS items and evaluate it on cs items, and vice versa. The asymmetry | | cs → \to anti-CS accuracy − - anti-CS → \to cs accuracy | | is 0.006 0.006 (see Table 3 )—smaller than the bootstrap error bar, and far below any threshold that would indicate overfitting. Both cross-direction probes attain ≥ 0.969 \geq 0.969 , matching the within-split CV values ( 0.975 ± 0.023 0.975\pm 0.023 and 0.994 ± 0.013 0.994\pm 0.013 ). This symmetry rules out the hypothesis that the probe is learning a surface marker specific to commonsense vocabulary.

sections.heading: Mixed training.
sections.text: Training on the cs + + anti-CS pool ( N = 320 N{=}320 ) and evaluating on CounterBench gives 0.800 0.800 (adjacent) / 0.919 0.919 (transitive), on par with the commonsense-only transfer. Mixing in anti-CS items neither degrades nor substantially improves cross-dataset transfer, confirming that the domain gap is benchmark-level rather than subset-level.

sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: The commonsense-only condition shows the readout direction is not a CLadder-specific surface marker: a probe fitted on CLadder real-world entities transfers at 0.844 0.844 – 0.913 0.913 to CounterBench’s nonsense-entity prompts. The anti-commonsense-only condition shows the probe is symmetric : anti-commonsense training yields the same direction as commonsense training. The mixed-training condition shows mixed training does not produce mixed signals. Together, these results support the main claim that the probed direction encodes an abstract causal-direction signal rather than a dataset-specific or subset-specific lexical artifact. Exp. sections.text: Qwen2.5-Instruct ≤ 14 \leq 14 B, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and DeepSeek-LLM-7B-Chat are loaded in bfloat16. sections.heading: Hardware.
sections.text: All experiments ran on a single node combining 10 × 10\times RTX 4090 GPUs ( 48 48 GB each) for the ≤ 14 \leq 14 B checkpoints and 4 × 4\times H20 GPUs ( 96 96 GB HBM3 each, with device_map=auto sharding) for the NF4-quantized 32B and 72B models. No training infrastructure (multi-node fabric, optimizer state shards, gradient communication) is used.

sections.heading: Models and quantization.
sections.text: We audit nine instruction-tuned checkpoints in total (Qwen2.5-Instruct at 0.5 0.5 B, 1.5 1.5 B, 3 3 B, 7 7 B, 14 14 B, 32 32 B, 72 72 B; DeepSeek-LLM-7B-Chat; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3); the scaling curve in Figure 3 uses the eight Qwen and Mistral checkpoints. Checkpoints with ≥ 32 \geq 32 B parameters are loaded with bitsandbytes NF4 4 4 -bit double-quantization and bfloat16 compute dtype; all other checkpoints are loaded in bfloat16.

sections.heading: Operations.
sections.text: The pipeline is inference-only : forward passes extract last-prompt-token hidden states and read the next-token Yes/No logits. The only learned object across the entire paper is the per-layer logistic probe. No fine-tuning, no gradient updates to the language model weights, no PEFT/LoRA, and no parameter modification of any released checkpoint is performed.

sections.heading: Total cost.
sections.text: The full suite—per-layer probe scans on ≥ 8 \geq 8 models, anti-CS scaling curve, six hard-negative families ( N = 24 N{=}24 each), six readout interfaces, head-level ablation map ( 28 × 28 28{\times}28 cells), and B = 10,000 B{=}10{,}000 paired bootstrap—totals approximately 120 120 aggregated GPU-hours (per-block breakdown in Table 19 ). Per-sample inference latency at max_new_tokens = 32 =32 and batch 1 1 is ∼ \sim 0.4 0.4 s ( 7 7 B in bf16), ∼ \sim 0.8 0.8 s ( 14 14 B in bf16), and ∼ \sim 3.2 3.2 s ( 72 72 B in NF4 with 4 4 -way sharding).

sections.heading: Energy and carbon.
sections.text: At an estimated ∼ \sim 0.4 0.4 kWh per GPU-hour averaged across the mixed RTX 4090 / H20 node, 120 120 GPU-hours consume ∼ \sim 48 48 kWh of raw GPU energy; with a datacenter PUE of 1.5 1.5 this becomes ∼ \sim 72 72 kWh of wall-plug consumption. Using a grid carbon intensity of 581 581 g CO 2 eq/kWh, this corresponds to ∼ \sim 42 42 kg CO 2 eq, several orders of magnitude below the cost of pre-training a single ≥ 7 \geq 7 B checkpoint.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: To address why the A/B-edge interface achieves near-perfect accuracy on anti-CS items while ordinary Yes/No fails at chance, we compute the selected-token binary entropy from the stored per-item logits in the readout-sweep pilots. For each item i i and interface, we extract the log-probabilities ℓ 0 ( i ) \ell_{0}^{(i)} and ℓ 1 ( i ) \ell_{1}^{(i)} of the two candidate tokens, normalise to obtain probabilities ( p 0 ( i ) , p 1 ( i ) ) (p_{0}^{(i)},p_{1}^{(i)}) , and compute the binary interface entropy H ( i ) = − p 0 ( i ) ​ log ⁡ p 0 ( i ) − p 1 ( i ) ​ log ⁡ p 1 ( i ) , H^{(i)}=-p_{0}^{(i)}\log p_{0}^{(i)}-p_{1}^{(i)}\log p_{1}^{(i)}, where the base is e e (nats) and ln ⁡ 2 ≈ 0.693 \ln 2\approx 0.693 is the maximum. For the Yes/No interface ( cause_fwd_yesno ), token 0 0 is the anti-CS-correct Yes answer and token 1 1 is No; the gold label is always 0 0 . For the A/B-edge interface ( ab_choose_causal_direction ), token 0 0 is option A (the correct direction) and token 1 1 is option B.

sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: Two complementary patterns explain the A/B saturation vs. Yes/No failure: (1) Yes/No failure is not mere hesitation—it is a confident wrong commit. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 41.3 % 41.3\% of anti-CS items have Yes/No interface entropy H < 0.1 H<0.1 nats, meaning the model assigns over 97 % 97\% probability mass to one token. That token is overwhelmingly No (the commonsense direction): mean p ⁡ ( Yes ) = 0.203 p(\text{Yes})=0.203 . Only 16.3 % 16.3\% of items show genuine uncertainty ( H > 0.5 H>0.5 nats = 0.72 ​ ln ⁡ 2 =0.72\ln 2 ). The low entropy is thus a wrong-direction lock-in , not a random or chance regime. For Qwen2.5-14B, this is even sharper: 72.5 % 72.5\% of items have H < 0.1 H<0.1 nats yet accuracy is only 0.450 0.450 —the model is highly confident but systematically wrong. (2) A/B saturation is near-zero-entropy correct-direction commitment. For Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 86.3 % 86.3\% of anti-CS items have A/B entropy H < 0.1 H<0.1 nats and mean accuracy is 1.000 1.000 . The model assigns ≥ 97 % {\geq}97\% probability to the correct edge direction across most items. The A/B interface bypasses the verbal Yes/No register and its associated commonsense prior by framing the task as a structural comparison between two explicit directed-edge descriptions; the model’s internal direction signal (linear probe Acc \mathrm{Acc} 0.994 0.994 at layer 8 8 ) is fully expressed without interference from the Yes/No commonsense prior.

sections.heading: Multi-token verbal commitment cascade.
sections.text: The low Yes/No entropy in instruction-tuned models also implies a multi-token commitment effect: once the first generated token is No (committed with ≥ 80 % {\geq}80\% probability), subsequent tokens fill in a causal explanation consistent with the commonsense direction (“No, because …”), amplifying the initial wrong commit. The structured A/B first token commits instead to the correct directed edge, after which any free-form continuation stays consistent with the in-prompt evidence. Accuracy values are annotated above each bar. A/B-edge entropy is far below Yes/No entropy for every model, while A/B accuracy is near 1.0 1.0 —a token-level signature of interface-side commitment failure: the model’s internal causal direction signal (probe Acc ≥ 0.94 \geq 0.94 ) is expressed at near-zero entropy in the A/B register but is overwhelmed by a confident wrong commit in the Yes/No register.

sections.text: Building on the finite-power null of the scalar V cs V_{\mathrm{cs}} swap ( Section 5.2 ), we test full-state injection on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at ℓ ⋆ = 27 \ell^{\star}{=}27 (last transformer block). We start from the N = 42 N{=}42 anti-CS items the model gets wrong on the ordinary Yes/No interface (so baseline accuracy is exactly 0 0 ) and from 41 41 commonsense items the model gets right (donors). Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2605.25891v1 [cs.CL] 25 May 2026 Causal Tongue-Tie: LLMs Can Encode Causal Direction, But Their Yes/No Outputs Fail to Express Ziyi Ding Affiliation: Tsinghua Shenzhen International Affiliation: Graduate School, Tsinghua University Affiliation: Shenzhen, China Xiao-Ping Zhang † † thanks: Corresponding author: xpzhang@ieee.org Affiliation: Tsinghua Shenzhen International Affiliation: Graduate School, Tsinghua University Affiliation: Shenzhen, China Abstract We find a mismatch between what large language models encode about a causal question and what they answer. On anti-commonsense CLadder ( Jin et al., 2023 ) items, a fixed linear probe recovers the evidence-supported answer from the model’s hidden state (accuracy ≈ 0.97 {\approx}0.97 ), while the spoken Yes/No reverts to the commonsense one (accuracy ≈ 0.5 {\approx}0.5 ). We call this Δ ≈ + 0.5 \Delta{\approx}{+}0.5 gap Causal Tongue-Tie : a wrong Yes/No decomposes into two separable failure modes—no internal signal vs. a signal the verbal interface cannot say. The implication cuts both ways for output-only causal benchmarks: a benchmark “correct” need not mean the model has understood, and a benchmark “wrong” need not mean it cannot. Sweeping claims about whether LLMs can do causal reasoning, drawn from a single accuracy number, deserve a second look. 1 Introduction We find that on causal Yes/No questions, large language models (LLMs) can encode an evidence-consistent causal direction in their hidden states that the ordinary Yes/No output does not say—a mismatch we call Causal Tongue-Tie ( Section 3 formalises “encode”). Background. Whether LLMs reason or merely produce fluent causal language is contested ( Bender et al., 2021 ; Zečević et al., 2023 ) . Benchmarks like CLadder ( Jin et al., 2023 ) and CounterBench ( Chen et al., 2025 ) score models by Yes/No accuracy on causal queries; probe studies report mixed evidence about the hidden state ( Chi et al., 2024 ; Geiger et al., 2025 ) . Motivation. On a CLadder anti-commonsense item stipulating “smoking prevents lung cancer”, Qwen2.5-7B answers “No” but a linear probe on the same hidden state returns “Yes”. The internal state tracks the stipulation; the spoken answer reverts to prior. This resonates with the Causal Parrots concern ( Zečević et al., 2023 ) : fluent causal language need not mean causal reasoning. But a wrong Yes/No alone cannot tell us if the model lacks causal knowledge or has it but cannot say it. Our contribution is Causal Tongue-Tie : the empirical finding that hidden states encode the evidence-aligned causal answer while the spoken Yes/No reverts to commonsense (on anti-CS CLadder : Acc probe ≈ 0.97 \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{probe}}\!\approx\!0.97 vs. Acc out ≈ 0.50 \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{out}}\!\approx\!0.50 ). In a 2 × 2 2{\times}2 view of “wrong on a causal benchmark” by internal signal × \times external Yes/No ( Figure 1 ), this dissociation occupies the off-diagonal cell (b) that has not been systematically studied. Code, prompts, hidden-state artifacts, and per-item probe logits and Yes/No probabilities accompany the public release. 2 Related Work Our finding sits at the intersection of two empirical lines: studies that compare hidden-state content with the model’s text output, and the broader concern that fluent causal language need not reflect causal reasoning. Hidden state vs. output. Several studies report that activations can contain information the textual answer does not faithfully express: Contrast-Consistent Search ( Burns et al., 2023 ) , inference-time intervention and truth-geometry directions ( Li et al., 2023 ; Marks and Tegmark, 2023 ) , and self-knowledge work ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ) . The same probe–output gap appears in clinical triage and hallucination detection ( Basu et al., 2026 ; CH-Wang et al., 2024 ) , and chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness work shows the explanation text can be a poor witness to the computation that produced the answer ( Lanham et al., 2023 ; Turpin et al., 2023 ) . Where we sit. Prior work isolates either side: hidden state alone (probing / CCS / latent-knowledge) or output alone (causal-benchmark accuracy). We add a measurement protocol that pairs them on a causal task where the two sides reliably disagree, separating a wrong Yes/No on CLadder from a missing internal signal. Anti-commonsense items provide the trigger, and wording-matched hard-negative controls rule out the surface-wording explanation rarely tested in prior latent-knowledge work. Causal Parrots and causal benchmarks. Bender et al. (2021) and the Causal Parrots sharpening ( Zečević et al., 2023 ) warn that LLMs may produce causal-looking answers by tracking surface regularities rather than causal evidence. Causal LLM benchmarks ( Jin et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Frohberg and Binder, 2022 ; Chi et al., 2024 ) operationalise this concern through output-side accuracy; we add a second axis: an internal readout channel from which an evidence-consistent direction is recoverable while the Yes/No does not express it. We use standard probing and direction-erasure tools ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ; Belrose et al., 2023 ; Feder et al., 2021 ; Zou et al., 2023 ) as measurement instruments, not as our contribution. 3 The Finding External Yes/No matches evidence External Yes/No contradicts evidence Internal: probe finds the direction (a) Aligned correct. Both readouts pick the evidence-supported answer. (b) ★ \bigstar Causal Tongue-Tie (this paper). Probe finds the evidence-aligned answer; Yes/No reverts to commonsense. Internal: probe finds nothing (c) ♢ \diamondsuit Causal Parrot risk. Right Yes/No by surface heuristic; no internal evidence-direction. (d) Genuine failure. Neither readout carries the evidence-supported answer. Figure 1: A 2 × \times 2 framework for a wrong Yes/No on a causal benchmark. The two off-diagonal cells— Causal Tongue-Tie (b, this paper) and the “Causal Parrot” (c, Zečević et al. 2023 )—are what output-only accuracy hides when it collapses (a)+(c) into “correct” and (b)+(d) into “failed”. The central finding is that a wrong Yes/No on a causal benchmark splits into four states ( Figure 1 ) by internal signal vs. external answer. Among these, the cell we call Causal Tongue-Tie —(b), probe finds the evidence-aligned answer, but the spoken Yes/No reverts to commonsense —is the failure mode output-only accuracy hides: the hidden state knows, the answer does not say so. Our paper is about (b). The rest of this section fixes the setting and notation ( Section 3.1 ), pins down what we mean by encode ( Section 3.2 ), states how we quantify the gap ( Section 3.3 ), and lists the empirical claims we will test in Section 3.4 ; a representative cell-(b) item is illustrated in Figure 2 . Figure 2: Cell (b) on one anti-CS item. From the same hidden state, the probe recovers NO ( Acc probe ≈ 0.97 \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{probe}}{\approx}0.97 ) while lm_head produces YES ( Acc out ≈ 0.50 \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{out}}{\approx}0.50 ); the Δ ≈ + 0.5 \Delta{\approx}{+}0.5 gap is the empirical handle on Causal Tongue-Tie . 3.1 Setting and notation To make Causal Tongue-Tie precise, we need a single forward pass on which we can read two things side by side: what the hidden state contains, and what the model says out loud. We therefore work with a frozen instruction-tuned transformer decoder f θ f_{\theta} with L L residual blocks. For each prompt x i x_{i} we read the activation 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ d \bm{h}_{i}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} after block ℓ \ell at the last prompt token position, and on the same pass we read the next-token Yes / No \textsf{Yes}/\textsf{No} probabilities through the model’s own unembedding lm_head : ℝ d → ℝ | 𝒱 | \texttt{lm\_head}\!:\!\mathbb{R}^{d}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|} . Our linear probe (defined below) reads 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) \bm{h}_{i}^{(\ell)} , and lm_head reads 𝒉 i ( L ) \bm{h}_{i}^{(L)} , both at the same token position, so on every item we can compare directly what is internally readable with what is actually said ( Appendix A gives a self-contained refresher on the decoder modules and residual stream). The items we audit are causal Yes/No questions, each with a gold answer. We write the dataset as 𝒟 = { ( x i , y i , c i , e i , b i , r i ) } i = 1 N , \mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i},c_{i},e_{i},b_{i},r_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, where x i x_{i} is the prompt, y i ∈ { Yes , No } y_{i}\in\{\textsf{Yes},\textsf{No}\} is the gold answer, ( c i , e i ) (c_{i},e_{i}) is the candidate cause–effect pair, and r i r_{i} marks the evidence type. A wrong Yes/No thus decomposes into two failure modes—no internal signal vs. an unexpressed one—not a single “failed” verdict. Implication for benchmark-based claims. The gap warns against output-only evaluation: hidden-state and Yes/No verdicts can differ by Δ ≈ + 0.5 \Delta{\approx}{+}0.5 , while prompt form also matters ( Appendix O ). Single-number claims conflate all three. Limitations Scope of the claim. Causal Tongue-Tie is an empirical diagnostic of a mismatch between hidden-state evidence and the final Yes/No answer. Following the operational definition in Section 3 , we claim that the model encodes causal direction only in that narrow sense, not human-like understanding, complete causal reasoning, or a causal circuit; the direction is causally sufficient on > 50 % {>}50\% but not all items the ordinary interface gets wrong ( Appendix N ). Scope of the finding. Our gap is a hidden-state-vs-output mismatch on textual causal questions (a short story plus a Yes/No probe). It is not a finding about causal discovery from raw observational data such as physical sensor readings, time-series, or experimental measurements; those tasks have very different inputs and evaluation, and lie outside our scope. A local contamination heuristic ( Table 18 ) reports anti-CS marker rate = 0.000 =0.000 and ns / CounterBench nonsense-entity coverage = 1.000 =1.000 , so the audited items are unlikely to be verbatim pretraining text; a rigorous n n -gram contamination audit is left to future work. The original direction label in Section 5.1 is partly confounded with question format, so the controlled hard-negative diagnostic—not the Section 5.1 probe alone—anchors the readout claim.
